span.label: whether the information a parietal neuron's firing rate carries about an upcoming choice depends on when in the ongoing population rhythm the spikes occur
span.quote: We test how the encoding of choice in a key decision-making node, the posterior parietal cortex (PPC), depends on the temporal structure of the surrounding population activity. We recorded spiking and local field potential (LFP) activity in the PPC while two rhesus macaques performed a decision-making task. We quantified the mutual information that neurons carried about an upcoming choice and its dependence on LFP activity.

span.label: whether and how the coding of decisions depends on the temporally structured firing of parietal neurons
span.quote: Previous studies have shown that coherently active ensembles of cells in the PPC predict reaction times ( 9 ) and movement choices ( 13 , 21 ) better than neurons without coherent dynamics. However, whether and how the coding of decisions depends on the temporally structured firing of PPC neurons remains unknown.

span.label: choice information is modulated by beta and gamma phase, and for beta it peaks at a different phase from the spike count, so information and excitability come apart
span.quote: Choice information contained in neural firing varied with the phase of beta and gamma activity. For gamma activity, maximum choice information occurred at the same phase as the maximum spike count. However, for beta activity, choice information and spike count were greatest at different phases.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: We test how the encoding of choice in a key decision-making node, the posterior parietal cortex (PPC), depends on the temporal structure of the surrounding population activity.

span.label: phase-dependent coding of choice in posterior parietal cortex
span.quote: We hypothesize that the encoding of decisions in the PPC should depend on the temporal structure present in neuronal activity.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We recorded spiking and local field potential (LFP) activity in the PPC while two rhesus macaques performed a decision-making task.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: An asymmetric interplay of excitation and inhibition within the beta cycle produces an uninformative upswing and an informative downswing of spiking
span.quote: Our results thus suggest that beta spiking in the PPC results from an asymmetric interaction between excitation and inhibition, producing a relatively less informative upswing and a more informative downswing of activity with similar activity magnitudes.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Beta rhythms are tuned to large-scale network communication rather than local processing, which is why choice information becomes separated in time from local excitability
span.quote: In contrast, beta activity may be tuned to larger network scales, leading to a separation between choice information and excitability.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Downstream ensembles read out the two rhythms with different integration windows, beta's extending past the moment of peak synchronous input to catch the later information peak
span.quote: Although the gamma activity may be most informative when spiking is greatest, the integration period for the beta activity may extend past the time of greatest synchronous activity to include a later period of peak information.

span.label: beta spiking is proposed to come from an asymmetric interplay of excitation and inhibition, giving an uninformative upswing and an informative downswing at similar spike counts
span.quote: Our results thus suggest that beta spiking in the PPC results from an asymmetric interaction between excitation and inhibition, producing a relatively less informative upswing and a more informative downswing of activity with similar activity magnitudes.

span.label: the two bands are read as two network scales, gamma as local bottom-up processing and beta as top-down linkage to a larger cortical network
span.quote: Specifically, gamma activity may reflect bottom-up–driven local processing, and beta activity may reflect top-down–driven processes that link local information to processing on a larger cortical scale ( 31 , 49 – 52 ). The coherent relationship we observe between the gamma and beta activity suggests that decision signals in the PPC arise in the interaction between these two types of influences.

span.label: downstream ensembles may integrate over different windows in the two bands, with the beta window reaching past peak synchrony to the later information peak
span.quote: Our findings are consistent with this view and suggest that beta and gamma activity may differ in the window of integration by downstream ensembles. Although the gamma activity may be most informative when spiking is greatest, the integration period for the beta activity may extend past the time of greatest synchronous activity to include a later period of peak information.

span.label: theta may regulate the faster scales, since theta phase predicts beta and gamma amplitude
span.quote: We found significant PAC between theta phases and beta amplitudes (permutation test, P < 10 −4 ) ( Fig. 4 A ). PAC for theta phases and gamma amplitudes (permutation test, P = 0.031) and beta phases and gamma amplitudes (permutation test, P < 10 −4 ) also was significant, albeit weaker (permutation tests, theta–beta vs. theta–gamma, P = 0.007; theta–beta vs. beta–gamma, P = 0.01; theta–gamma vs. beta–gamma, P = 0.48). In addition we found significant phase concentrations for the preferred PAC phases for the theta–beta and theta–gamma frequency combinations across the electrode pairs (Rayleigh tests: theta–beta, P < 10 −5 ; theta–gamma, P = 0.007) ( Fig. 4 A ). We found no significant concentration of the preferred PAC phase for the beta–gamma coupling (Rayleigh test, P = 0.22). Thus, the different time scales of PPC activity were nested with each other, with slower phases predicting faster amplitudes.

span.label: parietal spiking may multiplex decision signals into a beta and a gamma channel
span.quote: An intriguing possibility is that PPC spiking may multiplex decision signals into beta and gamma channels

span.label: How the beta-band dissociation between spiking and information is generated, and how downstream populations could read it out, is left open.
span.quote: The dissociation that we observe between spike counts and choice information for beta activity raises questions about how the activity can be generated and how other neuronal populations can decode such activity efficiently.

span.label: the proposed source of the beta dissociation - the beta to gamma phase difference - was tested and did not correlate with it
span.quote: The beta–gamma phase difference seemed to match roughly the dissociation of the moment of the choice-MI from spiking for beta activity. However, we observed no correlation between the beta–gamma phase difference and the moment of the beta choice-MI phase histogram on a single-spike LFP level

span.label: the primary modulation statistic assumes a single concentration across phase bins and cannot see multimodal modulation, so a second statistic had to be run
span.quote: Because the mean resultant length R assumes a unimodal concentration of quantities across phase bins, it is insensitive to more complex forms of modulation such as multimodal modulations. Thus we repeated the analysis of modulation strength across frequencies using permutation statistics based on the entropy (nonuniformity) H of the phase-dependent histogram

span.quote: MI estimation may have been biased by the differing spike counts at different phases of activity. We reestimated MI while stratifying spike counts to be equal across phase bins ( SI Materials and Methods ). The pattern of modulated choice-MI by beta and gamma activity persisted

span.label: the unit of analysis is mixed: 149 units of which only 45 are single units, the rest multiunit
span.quote: We analyzed the activity of 149 units [97 units (31 single units and 66 multiunits) for monkey C and 52 units (14 single units and 38 multiunits) for monkey R] and 186 simultaneously recorded local field potentials (LFP) (116 LFPs in monkey C and 70 LFPs in monkey R, one or two LFP electrodes per unit) from nearby (within ∼2 mm) electrodes.

span.label: gamma coherence depended on how far apart the two electrodes were, which is read as gamma being more local rather than as a recording artefact
span.quote: However, the distance between the electrode tips of the recording pairs influenced the SFC. Electrodes usually were separated from each other by about 2 mm during the recordings. Thus, gamma activity appeared to be more local than either theta or beta activity.

span.quote: We studied the encoding properties of neurons’ firing rates by quantifying the MI between the spiking of a neuron S and the movement condition C (in or out of response field) M I ( C , S ) = ∑ s , c P ( c ) P ( s | c ) l o g 2 ( P ( s | c ) P ( s ) ) . span.quote: In the beta-frequency band, the peak-to-trough modulation of spike counts was 13.6%, corresponding to a modulation in firing rate by about 6.6 spikes/s ( Fig. 3 B ). Measuring the spike counts for evenly spaced beta-activity phase bins allowed us to study the temporal concentration (trigonometric moment) of spiking in great detail (see radial black lines in Fig. 3 B – F ). The moment of the beta spike-count histogram was indistinguishable from the average spike-preferred beta phase during the analysis epoch, further indicating the symmetry of the distribution of spikes with beta-frequency phase.

span.label: a fitted psychometric function relating the reward difference between the two shapes to the probability of choosing one
span.quote: We recorded neuronal activity while monkeys performed reward-guided look-and-reach decisions. At the start of each trial, in the baseline epoch, the monkeys maintained touch and fixation on a central target. Then, in the choice epoch, they were presented with two alternatives, a circle and a triangle, and had to choose one with a combined look-and-reach movement ( Fig. 1 A ). We presented targets in two locations, randomly interleaved trial by trial. Both shapes were associated with changing reward magnitudes that presented a dynamic and challenging reward environment for the animals ( Fig. S1 ). Each monkey reliably allocated its choices according to the shapes’ relative reward magnitudes

span.label: THE ESTIMATOR'S OWN BIAS WOULD HAVE PRODUCED THE RESULT: mutual information runs high on small samples, the number of spikes differs from phase bin to phase bin, so phase-dependent information is exactly what a biased estimator would manufacture here

We quantified the information about upcoming movements in the firing rate by estimating the mutual information (MI) between the movement choice and the firing rate ( Fig. 1 D ). A total of 101 units (68%; 68 units for monkey C and 33 units for monkey R) exhibited significant choice-MI in the choice epoch (200–1,000 ms after choice target onset) (permutation tests, P < 0.05).

span.label: single units —operationalised-as→ spike waveforms
span.quote: To isolate single-unit activity, we projected spike waveforms into a 3D principal component feature space on a moving 100-s time window. We used the unsupervised clustering algorithm k -means to over-cluster the spike waveforms. We then manually merged clusters that displayed clear separation from the multiunit cloud. Only time periods during the recording in which the single-unit cluster was clearly isolated from the multiunit cloud over the entire 100-s time window were accepted as single units.

span.label: single units —part-of→ temporal structure
span.quote: Given the presence of activity at three distinct time scales, we wondered whether the activities co-occurred more often than would be expected by chance during the choice period. We found that 79 units [17 single units (38%) and 62 multiunits (60%)] were coherent both in the theta and beta ranges (Fisher’s exact test, P FWER = 2.27 × 10 −8 ), 40 units [eight single units (18%), 32 multiunits (31%)] were coherent in the theta and gamma ranges (Fisher’s exact test, P FWER = 0.0052), and 42 units [10 single units (22%) and 32 multiunits (31%)] were coherent in the beta and gamma ranges (Fisher’s exact test, P FWER = 6.53 × 10 −5 ). Thus, the units in the PPC often displayed temporal structure across multiple time scales.

span.label: theta activity —part-of→ temporal structure
span.quote: Thus, PPC spiking contains temporal structure at three time scales—theta, beta, and gamma—that respond differently to choice. During choice, theta activity remained constant, beta activity decreased, and gamma activity increased.

span.quote: Overall, we identified three interrelated temporal modes of neuronal activity in the PPC. Beta activity took a central role and was most prominently coupled to slower theta activity through PAC and to faster gamma activity through phase–phase coupling.

To estimate the orthogonal-MI, we removed the spike-count histogram’s prediction about the shape of the choice-MI histogram for each unit through regression ( Fig. 3 D and Fig. S4 ). The orthogonal-MI histogram was significantly modulated (permutation test, P < 10 −4 ). Thus, beta activity independently correlated with the spike counts and choice encoding of PPC units.

span.label: coherent
span.quote: Based on these tests, we labeled a unit as coherent if at least one frequency bin exhibited significant SFC. Where we recorded LFP activity on multiple electrodes, we chose the LFP recording with the maximum number of significant SFC frequency bins for further analyses.

span.label: stratifying
span.quote: To control for confounding associations between the amount of spiking and MI, we also performed the above analysis while stratifying the number of spikes at each phase bin. To do so, we randomly deleted spikes in excess of the minimum observed spike count across phase bins and then computed the MI at a given phase bin. We repeated this procedure 1,000 times and averaged the observed MI at each phase bin.

span.label: single units
span.quote: To isolate single-unit activity, we projected spike waveforms into a 3D principal component feature space on a moving 100-s time window. We used the unsupervised clustering algorithm k -means to over-cluster the spike waveforms. We then manually merged clusters that displayed clear separation from the multiunit cloud. Only time periods during the recording in which the single-unit cluster was clearly isolated from the multiunit cloud over the entire 100-s time window were accepted as single units.

span.label: LFP phase bin (eight evenly spaced bins)
span.term: LFP phase bin (eight evenly spaced bins)
span.quote: We defined eight different LFP phase bins and calculated how much choice-MI varies across the different bins ( Fig. 3 A ).

span.label: movement choice (target in or out of the neuron's response field)
span.term: movement choice (target in or out of the neuron's response field)
span.quote: We studied the encoding properties of neurons’ firing rates by quantifying the MI between the spiking of a neuron S and the movement condition C (in or out of response field)

span.label: reward magnitude associated with each target shape
span.term: reward magnitude associated with each target shape
span.quote: The mean reward magnitudes for each shape remained constant for 50–60 trials and then transitioned to a new mean magnitude in an unsignaled fashion ( Fig. S1 ).

span.label: choice mutual information carried by a unit's firing
span.term: choice mutual information carried by a unit's firing
span.quote: We quantified the information about upcoming movements in the firing rate by estimating the mutual information (MI) between the movement choice and the firing rate ( Fig. 1 D ).

span.label: spike-field coherence
span.quote: We next assessed the temporal structure of PPC activity by estimating the spike-field coherence (SFC) and LFP power spectra.

span.label: spike count per phase bin (stratified to equality)
span.term: spike count per phase bin (stratified to equality)
span.quote: We reestimated MI while stratifying spike counts to be equal across phase bins ( SI Materials and Methods ).

span.label: trial-locked evoked potentials
span.quote: We removed the influence of trial-locked evoked potentials through regression from each trial before further analysis.

span.label: choice-MI
span.quote: Choice-MI varied significantly with LFP phases in the beta- and gamma-frequency ranges (permutation tests, P FWER < 0.05) ( Fig. 3 A ) but not with theta phases. Repeating the analysis based on modulation entropy, which makes fewer distributional assumptions, yielded similar results ( SI Materials and Methods and Fig. S3 B ). The information that PPC units carried in their firing rates varied along phases in beta and gamma frequencies.

span.label: spike count
span.quote: In the beta-frequency band, the peak-to-trough modulation of spike counts was 13.6%, corresponding to a modulation in firing rate by about 6.6 spikes/s ( Fig. 3 B ). Spiking was distributed symmetrically about the spike-preferred beta-phase with no significant differences in the amount of spiking between the bins before and after the spike-preferred beta-phase (permutation test, P = 0.99). Measuring the spike counts for evenly spaced beta-activity phase bins allowed us to study the temporal concentration (trigonometric moment) of spiking in great detail (see radial black lines in Fig. 3 B – F ). The moment of the beta spike-count histogram was indistinguishable from the average spike-preferred beta phase during the analysis epoch, further indicating the symmetry of the distribution of spikes with beta-frequency phase.

span.label: SFC
span.quote: Beta activity varied with task epoch. SFC and power ( Fig. 2 A , Inset ) decreased significantly during the choice epoch compared with the baseline epoch

span.label: phase
span.quote: We defined eight different LFP phase bins and calculated how much choice-MI varies across the different bins ( Fig. 3 A ). We analyzed the choice epoch 200–1,000 ms after choice target onset and included all units that exhibited significant SFC and significant choice-MI during the choice epoch [79 units (53%); 54 units for monkey C and 25 units for monkey R). The period of 200–1,000 ms covered the choice epoch, avoiding visual onset transients present in the first 200 ms of PPC activity.

span.label: trigonometric moment
span.quote: In the beta-frequency band, the peak-to-trough modulation of spike counts was 13.6%, corresponding to a modulation in firing rate by about 6.6 spikes/s ( Fig. 3 B ). Spiking was distributed symmetrically about the spike-preferred beta-phase with no significant differences in the amount of spiking between the bins before and after the spike-preferred beta-phase (permutation test, P = 0.99). Measuring the spike counts for evenly spaced beta-activity phase bins allowed us to study the temporal concentration (trigonometric moment) of spiking in great detail (see radial black lines in Fig. 3 B – F ). The moment of the beta spike-count histogram was indistinguishable from the average spike-preferred beta phase during the analysis epoch, further indicating the symmetry of the distribution of spikes with beta-frequency phase.

span.label: 149 units — total number of recorded parietal units analyzed across the two monkeys
span.quote: We analyzed the activity of 149 units [97 units (31 single units and 66 multiunits) for monkey C and 52 units (14 single units and 38 multiunits) for monkey R] and 186 simultaneously recorded local field potentials (LFP) (116 LFPs in monkey C and 70 LFPs in monkey R, one or two LFP electrodes per unit) from nearby (within ∼2 mm) electrodes.

span.label: 101 units (68%) — number and share of units with significant choice mutual information during the choice epoch
span.quote: A total of 101 units (68%; 68 units for monkey C and 33 units for monkey R) exhibited significant choice-MI in the choice epoch (200–1,000 ms after choice target onset) (permutation tests, P < 0.05).

span.label: 13.6% / 6.6 spikes/s — peak-to-trough modulation of spike count by beta phase, and the equivalent firing-rate swing
span.quote: In the beta-frequency band, the peak-to-trough modulation of spike counts was 13.6%, corresponding to a modulation in firing rate by about 6.6 spikes/s ( Fig. 3 B ).

span.label: 15.3% — peak-to-trough modulation of choice mutual information by beta phase
span.quote: Choice-MI showed a peak-to-trough modulation by the beta activity of 15.3%.

span.label: 6.2% — peak-to-trough modulation of spiking by gamma phase (about three spikes/s)
span.quote: The peak-to-trough modulation of spiking along the gamma phases was 6.2%, corresponding to a firing rate modulation of approximately three spikes/s.

span.label: 12.3% — peak-to-trough modulation of choice mutual information by gamma phase
span.quote: Peak-to-trough modulation of choice-MI by gamma activity was 12.3%.

span.label: 16,123 trials (monkey C) and 11,440 trials (monkey R) — number of choice-task trials contributed by each animal
span.quote: The data analyzed here encompassed 16,123 trials (monkey C) and 11,440 trials (monkey R) that the animals performed on the choice task.

span.label: 1.07 mm vs. 2.86 mm — median electrode-tip separation of the near and far halves of recording pairs, used to test locality of the rhythms
span.quote: However, when comparing the SFC for the half of the recordings with electrode tips near each other (median separation of 1.07 mm) and the half of the recordings with far electrode tips farther apart (median separation of 2.86 mm), we found that higher-frequency SFC (>20 Hz), particularly including the gamma activity, was stronger for electrode tips that were closer to each other ( P FDR < 0.05) ( Fig. S2 E and F ).

span.label: r = −0.063, P = 0.55 — circular correlation between beta-gamma phase difference and the moment of the beta choice-MI histogram (no relationship)
span.quote: However, we observed no correlation between the beta–gamma phase difference and the moment of the beta choice-MI phase histogram on a single-spike LFP level (circular correlation, same electrode pairs from Fig. 3 ; n = 79, r = −0.063, P = 0.55).

span.label: 13.6% — peak-to-trough modulation of the spike count by beta phase, about 6.6 spikes per second
span.quote: In the beta-frequency band, the peak-to-trough modulation of spike counts was 13.6%, corresponding to a modulation in firing rate by about 6.6 spikes/s ( Fig. 3 B ). Spiking was distributed symmetrically about the spike-preferred beta-phase with no significant differences in the amount of spiking between the bins before and after the spike-preferred beta-phase (permutation test, P = 0.99). Measuring the spike counts for evenly spaced beta-activity phase bins allowed us to study the temporal concentration (trigonometric moment) of spiking in great detail (see radial black lines in Fig. 3 B – F ). The moment of the beta spike-count histogram was indistinguishable from the average spike-preferred beta phase during the analysis epoch, further indicating the symmetry of the distribution of spikes with beta-frequency phase.

span.label: 15.3% — peak-to-trough modulation of choice information by beta phase - a similar size to the spike modulation but at a different phase
span.quote: Choice-MI showed a peak-to-trough modulation by the beta activity of 15.3%. Unlike the spike counts, the choice-MI was asymmetric around the spike-preferred beta phase. The moment of the choice-MI histogram differed significantly from the moment of the beta spike-count histogram (permutation test, P < 10 −4 ) with MI peaking during the downswing of the spiking cycle ( Fig. 3 C ). In other words, spike count and choice-MI peaked at different times during the beta activity.

span.label: 12.3% — peak-to-trough modulation of choice information by gamma phase, against 6.2 percent for the spike count
span.quote: Peak-to-trough modulation of choice-MI by gamma activity was 12.3%. Choice-MI shared the same temporal concentration along gamma phases ( Fig. 3 F ). We found no difference between the moments of choice-MI and spike count in the gamma activity (permutation test, P = 0.59).

span.label: P = 0.30 — the gamma orthogonal-information null - the result that says gamma's two effects are not separable
span.quote: We then estimated the orthogonal-MI for gamma frequency activity ( Fig. 3 G ). The orthogonal-MI for gamma activity was distributed uniformly across phase bins (permutation test, P = 0.30). No phase bin exhibited differences from the average orthogonal-MI across gamma-phase bins (permutation tests, all P > 0.05). Thus, correlations between gamma activity, choice-MI, and spike counts were not independent.

span.label: r = −0.063 — the correlation between the beta-gamma phase difference and the moment of the beta choice-MI phase histogram, testing whether that coupling could contribute to the temporal localization of the choice-MI
span.quote: The beta–gamma phase difference seemed to match roughly the dissociation of the moment of the choice-MI from spiking for beta activity. Beta–gamma phase–phase coupling could contribute to the temporal localization of the choice-MI with respect to the beta activity. However, we observed no correlation between the beta–gamma phase difference and the moment of the beta choice-MI phase histogram on a single-spike LFP level

span.label: 149 units — 45 single units and 104 multiunits from two monkeys, with 186 simultaneous field recordings
span.quote: We analyzed the activity of 149 units [97 units (31 single units and 66 multiunits) for monkey C and 52 units (14 single units and 38 multiunits) for monkey R] and 186 simultaneously recorded local field potentials (LFP) (116 LFPs in monkey C and 70 LFPs in monkey R, one or two LFP electrodes per unit) from nearby (within ∼2 mm) electrodes.

span.label: 101 units (68%) — units with significant choice information in the firing rate
span.quote: As expected, the firing rate of PPC neurons robustly encoded the upcoming movement choice. After choice target onset, units exhibited a strong transient increase in the firing rate regardless of the upcoming movement choice ( Fig. 1 C ). Firing rates separated depending on the movement choice. We quantified the information about upcoming movements in the firing rate by estimating the mutual information (MI) between the movement choice and the firing rate ( Fig. 1 D ). A total of 101 units (68%; 68 units for monkey C and 33 units for monkey R) exhibited significant choice-MI in the choice epoch (200–1,000 ms after choice target onset) (permutation tests, P < 0.05).

span.label: 16,123 trials — trials from monkey C, against 11,440 from monkey R
span.quote: The data analyzed here encompassed 16,123 trials (monkey C) and 11,440 trials (monkey R) that the animals performed on the choice task.
